blocks.text: Boaz belongs to the judges-era world of harvest labor, household economy, kinship obligations, and concern for the continuity of family land. Ruth first encounters him as the owner of the field where she works, but Naomi recognizes another dimension of his identity: he belongs to Elimelech’s family and is one of their near kinsmen. The chapter thus places ordinary harvest work within a social setting where family relationships could carry substantial importance.

Gleaning—the work of gathering grain left behind by reapers—is portrayed here as survival labor. Ruth spends the day following the harvesters and later beats out what she has collected. Boaz’s help goes well beyond simply allowing her to gather leftovers: he gives her a safe place among his workers, access to their water, a shared meal, freedom to glean among the sheaves, and deliberately loosened grain. His repeated commands not to touch, reproach, rebuke, or confront her show that his provision includes protection as well as food.

The narrative repeatedly calls Ruth “the Moabitess,” keeping her foreign origin visible even after she has committed herself to Naomi, Naomi’s people, and Israel’s God. Ruth herself recognizes that her status makes Boaz’s favor remarkable. Some readers have proposed that the book directly responds to a particular later policy concerning intermarriage, but that historical proposal remains debated and should not be treated as certain.

Ruth places divine provision alongside concrete human action. Boaz speaks of Jehovah’s reward and refuge, and Naomi blesses Jehovah for continuing kindness; meanwhile, Ruth works, the reapers gather, Boaz gives protective instructions, and Naomi interprets what has happened. Across the book, food and conception are explicitly attributed to the Lord even though most of the plot advances through the decisions and labor of its human characters. This pattern helps explain why the chapter can present Ruth’s apparently chance arrival in Boaz’s field together with purposeful acts of generosity and faithfulness.

Within the book’s larger movement, this harvest chapter begins to answer the famine, bereavement, and emptiness of the opening. The story will continue from harvest toward kinship redemption, birth, communal blessing, and genealogy. Ruth 2 is therefore a major transition: Naomi and Ruth have not yet reached the story’s resolution, but food, relationship, and renewed possibility have entered their circumstances.
